definition: A graphics processing unit (GPU) is a specialized electronic circuit designed for digital image processing and to accelerate computer graphics, being present either as a component on a discrete graphics card or embedded on motherboards, mobile phones, personal computers, workstations, and game consoles.
details: GPUs are also increasingly being used for artificial intelligence (AI) processing and model training due to linear algebra acceleration, which is also used extensively in graphics processing. Although there is no single definition of the term, and it may be used to describe any video display system, in modern use a GPU includes the ability to internally perform the calculations needed for various graphics tasks, like rotating and scaling 3D images, and often the additional ability to run custom programs known as shaders. This contrasts with earlier graphics controllers known as video display controllers which had no internal calculation capabilities, or blitters, which performed only basic memory movement operations. The modern GPU emerged during the 1990s, adding the ability to perform operations like drawing lines and text without CPU help, and later adding 3D functionality. Graphics functions are generally independent and this lends these tasks to being implemented on separate calculation engines. Modern GPUs include hundreds, or thousands, of calculation units. This made them useful for non-graphic calculations involving embarrassingly parallel problems due to their parallel structure. The ability of GPUs to rapidly perform vast numbers of calculations has led to their adoption in diverse fields including artificial intelligence (AI) where they excel at handling data-intensive and computationally demanding tasks. Other non-graphical uses include the training of neural networks and cryptocurrency mining.

explainer.lead: A GPU is a specialized chip built to speed up image processing and computer graphics, and it is now also widely used for AI. Its many calculation units can handle large numbers of independent operations at once, making it useful for neural-network training and other computationally demanding work.

tiers.eli5: A GPU is like a team of many small helpers working on a big job at the same time. Drawing or changing a picture involves lots of separate calculations, so the helpers can each take some and finish the job faster. The same teamwork also helps computers train AI models and do other calculation-heavy tasks.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers use GPUs to accelerate graphics and AI workloads, especially neural-network training and linear-algebra operations with many independent calculations. Graphics applications can also run custom programs called shaders on the GPU. The main pitfall is assuming every workload will benefit: GPUs are best suited to parallel, data-intensive calculations rather than tasks that cannot be divided into independent work.
tiers.paperLevel: A GPU is a specialized electronic circuit for digital image processing and accelerated computer graphics; in modern usage, it performs graphics calculations internally and often executes custom programs called shaders. There is no single definition of the term, but modern GPUs contain hundreds or thousands of calculation units and are distinct from video display controllers and basic memory-movement blitters. Their AI advantage comes from parallel linear-algebra acceleration, with the clearest fit to data-intensive and embarrassingly parallel problems.

explainer.example: To rotate and scale a 3D image, a modern GPU performs the required graphics calculations internally rather than relying on the CPU for every operation. Its calculation units handle the independent work in parallel, and shaders can supply additional custom graphics processing.

usedIn.name: Computer graphics
usedIn.detail: Accelerates image processing and operations such as rotating and scaling 3D images.

usedIn.name: AI model training
usedIn.detail: Speeds up neural-network training and other data-intensive calculations through parallel linear algebra.

usedIn.name: Cryptocurrency mining
usedIn.detail: Uses the GPU's ability to perform vast numbers of calculations for a non-graphical workload.

usedIn.name: Game consoles and personal computers
usedIn.detail: Provides graphics acceleration either on a discrete graphics card or embedded in the device.

explainer.intuition: Many graphics calculations are independent, so they can be handled by separate calculation engines at the same time. A GPU applies that parallel structure to graphics and, increasingly, to AI and other numerical work.
howItWorks: The GPU receives graphics data or another suitable computational workload.
The work is divided into calculations that can proceed independently.
Hundreds or thousands of calculation units perform those operations in parallel; graphics tasks may also use custom shader programs.
The results produce processed images or numerical outputs, such as the calculations needed during neural-network training.
explainer.whyItMatters: GPUs made demanding graphics practical by accelerating large numbers of calculations. The same parallel structure now supports AI processing and neural-network training, as well as other non-graphical uses such as cryptocurrency mining.
misconceptions: A GPU is not limited to graphics: it can also accelerate AI training and other suitable numerical calculations.
Not every graphics-related device is a modern GPU; earlier video display controllers had no internal calculation capabilities, and blitters only performed basic memory movement.
A GPU does not make every task parallel; its strengths are most useful when calculations can be performed independently.
